To verify that the depth signal resides in the features rather than the classifier,
we repeat the 6-generator LOGO evaluation using Logistic Regression and Random Forest
in place of XGBoost (Table~\ref{tab:alt-classifier}).
All other settings (the same 7 features, 3-class labels, and class-balanced downsampling) are
kept identical. For Logistic Regression we apply standard scaling to the features.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{LOGO macro-F1 across three classifiers. Each column shows the held-out generator F1. (6-generator LOGO; 3-class.)}
\label{tab:alt-classifier}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lc cccccc}
\toprule
Classifier & Avg F1 & OLMo-2 & Py-1B & Py-2.8B & Qw-0.6B & Qw-1.7B & Qw-8B \\
\midrule
XGBoost          & 0.789 & 0.764 & 0.856 & 0.804 & 0.824 & 0.806 & 0.683 \\
Random Forest    & 0.790 & 0.764 & 0.856 & 0.804 & 0.825 & 0.807 & 0.684 \\
Logistic Regr.   & 0.725 & 0.719 & 0.781 & 0.740 & 0.745 & 0.743 & 0.624 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Both tree-based classifiers achieve LOGO F1 $\approx 0.79$,
and even a linear model reaches $0.725$, well above the $0.33$ chance baseline for
three classes.
The per-generator ranking is also consistent across classifiers
(Pythia-1B easiest, Qwen3-8B hardest),
confirming that discriminative power originates in the entropy and lexical features,
not in classifier capacity.

\subsection*{Sampling Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{app:sampling-sensitivity}

To assess robustness to decoding hyperparameters, we regenerate Qwen3-1.7B continuation chains under three sampling configurations (the remaining five generators retain their default-configuration data) and re-evaluate the 6-generator LOGO pipeline (Table~\ref{tab:sampling-ablation}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Depth classification under varying sampling parameters. All other settings match the default pipeline. (6-generator LOGO; 3-class and binary.)}
\label{tab:sampling-ablation}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc ccc}
\toprule
Config & Temp.\ & Top-$p$ & 3-class F1 & Binary F1 & $\rho$(entropy\_mean) \\
\midrule
Low        & 0.5 & 0.80 & 0.785 & 0.797 & $-0.694$ \\
Default    & 0.7 & 0.90 & 0.788 & 0.799 & $-0.602$ \\
High       & 1.0 & 0.95 & 0.726 & 0.733 & $-0.002$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The depth signal is robust to moderate sampling variation: low and default configurations differ by at most 0.3\,pp in both 3-class and binary F1, and entropy--depth Spearman correlations remain strongly negative ($\rho \leq -0.60$).
At high temperature ($t{=}1.0$, top-$p{=}0.95$), classification degrades by approximately 6\,pp and the entropy--depth correlation collapses to near zero ($\rho = -0.002$).
This is consistent with the hypothesis that depth features are shaped by the sampling mechanism (\S\ref{sec:discussion}): elevated temperature injects sufficient randomness to flatten the distributional drift that accumulates across generation steps, effectively masking the depth signal.
The practical implication is that depth fingerprinting applies reliably under standard decoding regimes but should not be expected to generalize to high-entropy sampling settings.

We complement the permutation importance analysis (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) with a leave-one-feature-out ablation. Each row drops one of the seven features and re-evaluates the full 6-gen LOGO protocol; $\Delta$ is the change relative to the full 7-feature ensemble (F1\,=\,0.789).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Dropped feature} & \textbf{LOGO F1} & $\boldsymbol{\Delta}$ \textbf{vs Full} \\
\midrule
entropy\_max    & 0.774 & $-$1.50\,pp \\
entropy\_mean   & 0.783 & $-$0.63\,pp \\
ttr             & 0.784 & $-$0.55\,pp \\
hapax\_ratio    & 0.785 & $-$0.42\,pp \\
tail\_decay     & 0.786 & $-$0.33\,pp \\
entropy\_std    & 0.786 & $-$0.29\,pp \\
entropy\_min    & 0.789 & $+$0.01\,pp \\
\midrule
Full (7 features) & 0.789 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Leave-one-feature-out ablation (6-gen LOGO). Each row drops one feature and re-evaluates with the LOGO protocol. Sorted by impact magnitude.}
\label{tab:lofo}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Analysis.}
Entropy\_max causes the largest degradation when removed ($-$1.5\,pp), despite ranking only fourth in permutation importance (split frequency 0.063). This indicates that entropy\_max provides unique signal (capturing the most surprising token under the reference model) that is not redundant with other features.
Conversely, entropy\_min is fully redundant ($\Delta$\,=\,+0.01\,pp), consistent with its near-zero permutation importance (0.015).
Six of seven features contribute positively to the ensemble, confirming that the 7-feature design is not over-specified.

10\%           & 0.614 & [0.599, 0.629] & 0.492 \\

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

At 10\% replacement, binary F1 remains 0.614, well above the 0.50 random baseline, indicating that depth signal survives moderate perturbation.

Three-class classification is more sensitive (0.737$\to$0.367 at 20\%), because distinguishing gen-0 from gen-1 relies heavily on lexical diversity features (TTR, hapax ratio) that are directly disrupted by word replacement.
The binary metric, which excludes gen-0, is inherently more robust since it depends primarily on reference-model entropy features distributed across many tokens.

At 20\% replacement, the 7-feature ensemble surpasses entropy-only on binary F1 (0.591 vs.\ 0.569), despite starting from a lower baseline.

Lexical features (TTR, hapax ratio), as document-level summary statistics, are more stable under per-word perturbation and act as stabilizers in the full ensemble.

1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Shape stationarity hypothesis.}
5	Upper-tail features remain near-stationary because the softmax architecture and sampling hyperparameters that determine distributional shape are fixed across depths; recursive generation shifts context toward high-probability regions (reducing entropy mean) without altering the generation mechanism itself.
6	This predicts stationarity until the model reaches its fixed-point distribution, a regime not observed at chain length $\leq$4.
7	Sampling ablation supports this: depth signal is robust at $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ (${\leq}0.3$\,pp degradation) but breaks down at $t = 1.0$ ($-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), where sampling noise dominates distributional shape.
8	
9	\paragraph{Prompt-type dependence.}
10	Continuation chains yield the strongest signal (F1\,=\,0.781 vs.\ 0.730 for elaboration), with cross-type transfer at 0.753 (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
11	Semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift, consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}.
12	
13	\paragraph{Practical applicability.}
14	At the document level, gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.64 (36\% misclassification) is insufficient for automated filtering but suitable for flagging; at the corpus level, error scales as $O(1/\sqrt{n})$, making aggregate depth composition estimates reliable.
15	
16	\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
17	Model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} describes degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs; our inference-chain drift occurs without parameter updates, representing an early, reversible stage of the same narrowing.
18	Topic drift accounts for $<$9\% of feature variance ($R^2 = 0.082$), confirming it mediates rather than confounds depth signal.
19	
20	\paragraph{Scope boundaries.}
21	Three classes represent the practical granularity ceiling: 5-class LOGO F1 drops to $\approx$0.49, with gen-2/gen-3 inseparable (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}); QLoRA fine-tuning recovers 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 (Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming signal beyond summary statistics.
22	Simulated text perturbation degrades binary F1 sublinearly (0.614 at 10\% replacement vs.\ 0.695 baseline; Appendix~\ref{app:human-edit}).
23	Instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.764 base), justifying our restriction to base models.
